The Cauchy Product

(∑an)(∑bn)=∑cn(\sum a_n)(\sum b_n) = \sum c_n(∑an​)(∑bn​)=∑cn​ with cn=∑k=0nakbn−kc_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_{n-k}cn​=∑k=0n​ak​bn−k​ — sweeping the lattice along diagonals. Mertens' theorem (absolute convergence on one side saves the product) and the counterexample when both converge only conditionally.

Multiplying and dividing by n!n!n! gives 1k!(n−k)!=1n!(nk)\frac{1}{k!(n-k)!} = \frac{1}{n!} \binom{n}{k}k!(n−k)!1​=n!1​(kn​), so cn=1n!∑k=0n(nk)c_n = \frac{1}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}cn​=n!1​∑k=0n​(kn​).
  2. By the binomial theorem (1+1)n=∑k=0n(nk)(1+1)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}(1+1)n=∑k=0n​(kn​), the inner sum is 2n2^n2n, so cn=2nn!c_n = \frac{2^n}{n!}cn​=n!2n​. The Cauchy-product series is therefore ∑n=0∞cn=∑n=0∞2nn!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{2^n}{n!}∑n=0∞​cn​=∑n=0∞​n!2n​, which is the exponential series at x=2x = 2x=2, summing to e2e^2e2.
  3. This computation is legitimate because the exponential series converges absolutely: the ratio test gives 1/(k+1)!1/k!=1k+1→0\frac{1/(k+1)!}{1/k!} = \frac{1}{k+1} \to 01/k!1/(k+1)!​=k+11​→0, so Mertens' theorem (problem 1) applies and yields ∑cn=e⋅e=e2\sum c_n = e \cdot e = e^2∑cn​=e⋅e=e2 — the series version of the exponent law e1⋅e1=e2e^1 \cdot e^1 = e^2e1⋅e1=e2.

Show proof

First, both factor series converge: ak=(−1)kk+1a_k = \frac{(-1)^k}{\sqrt{k+1}}ak​=k+1​(−1)k​ alternates in sign and 1k+1\frac{1}{\sqrt{k+1}}k+1​1​ decreases monotonically to 000, so Leibniz's test applies. But ∑∣ak∣=∑1k+1\sum |a_k| = \sum \frac{1}{\sqrt{k+1}}∑∣ak​∣=∑k+1​1​ is a ppp-series with p=12p = \frac12p=21​, hence diverges — the convergence is conditional.

The Cauchy-product term is cn=∑k=0n(−1)kk+1⋅(−1)n−kn−k+1=(−1)n∑k=0n1(k+1)(n−k+1)c_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{(-1)^k}{\sqrt{k+1}} \cdot \frac{(-1)^{n-k}}{\sqrt{n-k+1}} = (-1)^n \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{(k+1)(n-k+1)}}cn​=∑k=0n​k+1​(−1)k​⋅n−k+1​(−1)n−k​=(−1)n∑k=0n​(k+1)(n−k+1)​1​, so ∣cn∣=∑k=0n1(k+1)(n−k+1)|c_n| = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{(k+1)(n-k+1)}}∣cn​∣=∑k=0n​(k+1)(n−k+1)​1​.
  3. By AM-GM, (k+1)(n−k+1)≤((k+1)+(n−k+1)2)2=(n+22)2(k+1)(n-k+1) \leq \left(\frac{(k+1)+(n-k+1)}{2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{n+2}{2}\right)^2(k+1)(n−k+1)≤(2(k+1)+(n−k+1)​)2=(2n+2​)2. Hence each summand 1(k+1)(n−k+1)≥2n+2\frac{1}{\sqrt{(k+1)(n-k+1)}} \geq \frac{2}{n+2}(k+1)(n−k+1)​1​≥n+22​, and with n+1n+1n+1 summands, ∣cn∣≥(n+1)⋅2n+2=2(n+1)n+2|c_n| \geq (n+1)\cdot\frac{2}{n+2} = \frac{2(n+1)}{n+2}∣cn​∣≥(n+1)⋅n+22​=n+22(n+1)​. Since 2(n+1)n+2≥1\frac{2(n+1)}{n+2} \geq 1n+22(n+1)​≥1 for n≥0n \geq 0n≥0, ∣cn∣≥1|c_n| \geq 1∣cn​∣≥1 (in fact ∣cn∣→2|c_n| \to 2∣cn​∣→2).
  4. Since ∣cn∣≥1|c_n| \geq 1∣cn​∣≥1, cn↛0c_n \not\to 0cn​→0, and the nnn-th term test gives that ∑cn\sum c_n∑cn​ diverges. Two convergent series can have a divergent Cauchy product — absolute convergence of one factor in Mertens' theorem (problem 1) is not a removable hypothesis but an essential one.
